assigned.title: The Drizzle snapshot names three primary keys the database does not have
assigned.notes:
FOUND BY claude-backend WHILE REPAIRING PL-0406, PROPOSED FOR gpt-architect TO RULE ON. It is NOT
fixed there: PL-0406's acceptance says in terms that changing the schema and adding a second migration
are out of scope, and this needs one or the other.

THE FINDING, EXACT. PL-0406 installed `migrations/meta/0000_snapshot.json` so `drizzle-kit generate`
has a previous state to diff against -- without it the next `db:generate` emits a duplicate migration
re-creating all eight tables, which was measured. The snapshot is derived from the ORM schema in
`src/schema/index.ts`. Compared against the database the REVIEWED hand-written migration actually
produces, every foreign key and every unique constraint matches by name. THREE PRIMARY KEY NAMES DO
NOT:

  table                      live database name              snapshot expects
  active_profile_selection   active_profile_selection_pkey   active_profile_selection_session_id_pk
  playback_progress          playback_progress_pkey          playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk
  watchlist_entry            watchlist_entry_pkey            watchlist_entry_profile_id_content_id_pk

Measured against PostgreSQL 16.15: `pg_constraint` after `npm run db:migrate` on a fresh database,
against the `compositePrimaryKeys` keys in the installed snapshot.

WHY: the hand-written SQL writes `"session_id" text PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL` and
`CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_pkey" PRIMARY KEY (...)`, so PostgreSQL uses its own `_pkey` convention
or the stated name. Drizzle's `primaryKey()` synthesises `<table>_<cols>_pk`. Both describe the same
KEY; they disagree only about what it is CALLED.

WHY IT MATTERS LATER RATHER THAN NOW. Nothing is broken today: the schema is correct, all eight tables
exist, the constraints are enforced, and `generate` diffs the ORM schema against the snapshot without
ever consulting the database. The trap is the first migration that touches a primary key. Drizzle
would emit `ALTER TABLE "playback_progress" DROP CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk"`,
which does not exist, and the migration would fail against every real database -- in whatever
environment it ran first.

THREE WAYS OUT, unranked, for the ruling:
  (a) Name the constraints in the ORM schema so the snapshot matches the database -- `primaryKey({ name:
      "playback_progress_pkey", columns: [...] })`. Smallest, changes no SQL, leaves the reviewed
      migration untouched. Changes the schema file, which PL-0406 could not.
  (b) A second migration that renames the three constraints to Drizzle's convention. Changes a live
      database to suit a tool's naming, which is the wrong way round.
  (c) Hand-edit the snapshot's three names. Cheapest and worst: a snapshot is generated output, and a
      hand-edit is lost the next time anyone regenerates it.

(a) looks right from here and is NOT being taken unilaterally, because it edits the schema module that
PL-0405 reviewed and because the choice is exactly the kind PL-0406's acceptance reserved.

WHAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT AND DID NOT: `npm run db:check` answers "Everything's fine" -- it validates
the journal, not the agreement between the snapshot and a real database. Whatever remedy is chosen
should come with an assertion that compares generated constraint names against a migrated database, or
this recurs the next time a snapshot is produced.

typecheck.evidence:
`npm run typecheck` -> 22/22 turbo tasks. `npm run lint` -> 12/12, 0 errors. `npm run repo:validate` -> passed. `npx tsc --noEmit -p packages/persistence/tsconfig.json` clean.

WORTH RECORDING FOR THIS TASK SPECIFICALLY: `primaryKey({ name, columns })` is a typed overload rather than an extra property tolerated at runtime -- `drizzle-orm/pg-core/primary-keys.d.ts` declares `primaryKey(config: { name?: string; columns: [TColumn, ...TColumns] })`, so a misspelt key would be a compile error here rather than a silently ignored option. All three call sites already used the config form, so the change is one property each and nothing about the key, its columns or its behaviour moved.

unit.evidence:
`npm run test` -> 22/22 turbo tasks; @liberty/persistence 275 passed + 1 skipped (was 268), @liberty/web 1308, @liberty/provider-sdk 288, @liberty/catalog-ingestion 152, @liberty/recommendations 47, @liberty/backend 36.

THE NEW FILE IS `src/schema/constraint-names.test.ts`, 8 tests in two layers, and the second layer is the one gpt-architect's ruling required: "an assertion comparing the ORM/generated constraint names with the ACTUAL constraint names produced by a freshly migrated PostgreSQL database".

LAYER 1 -- ALWAYS RUNS, NO DATABASE. The snapshot's primary-key name for each of the three tables must be the name the reviewed migration produces. For `playback_progress` and `watchlist_entry` the migration states the name, so this is a file-to-file comparison against `CONSTRAINT "<name>" PRIMARY KEY`. For `active_profile_selection` the migration writes an inline `"session_id" text PRIMARY KEY` and the name is PostgreSQL's to choose, so layer 1 can only assert the convention -- which is exactly why layer 2 exists. A fourth table acquiring a primary key is caught too: the test enumerates every composite key in the snapshot and requires the set to equal the three.

LAYER 2 -- RUN AGAINST POSTGRESQL 16.15, and this is the gate's real evidence. Opt-in through
`LIBERTY_CONSTRAINT_CHECK_DATABASE_URL`; it REFUSES a database that already has tables rather than running DDL over someone's data. It applies the reviewed migration and reads `pg_constraint`:

  "user"                    user_pkey
  account                   account_pkey
  active_profile_selection  active_profile_selection_pkey
  playback_progress         playback_progress_pkey
  profile                   profile_pkey
  session                   session_pkey
  verification              verification_pkey
  watchlist_entry           watchlist_entry_pkey

All three of the named constraints agree with the snapshot, and the eight-table postcondition is asserted in the same transaction. Result: 8 passed, 0 skipped. In the unit job the live layer SKIPS -- the unit job has no PostgreSQL and the e2e job that does is outside this task's write surface -- so 1 skipped is the expected CI shape and the evidence above is how the claim was actually established.

PROVEN NON-VACUOUS BY MUTATION: reverting one snapshot name to Drizzle's synthesised
`playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk` turns BOTH layers red (2 failed, 6 passed); restoring it returns 8 green.

AND THE TWO POSTCONDITIONS THE RULING ASKED TO BE PRESERVED, measured after the change:
 - `npm run db:migrate -w @liberty/persistence` on a fresh database -> exit 0, 8 tables, constraint
   names exactly as listed above.
 - `drizzle-kit generate` against a copy of the migrations directory -> "No schema changes, nothing
   to migrate", so the regenerated snapshot is consistent with the schema and no duplicate migration
   is proposed.

The reviewed hand-written migration SQL and the journal are BYTE-IDENTICAL -- `git diff` reports no change to either. The only metadata that moved is 7 lines of `meta/0000_snapshot.json`, which are the three names.
